name: Analytics Dashboard
summary: One question per screen. A KPI row, one chart, one table — plus the empty, loading and error states that generated dashboards always skip.
lede: A dashboard is not a wall of charts. It is a screen where a specific person answers a specific question in under a minute. Every panel that does not serve that question costs attention that the answering panel needs.
brief: Generated dashboards share a signature: seven KPI cards of equal size, four charts with no axis units, and three rows of identical fake data. The layout looks plausible in a screenshot and collapses the moment real numbers arrive, because nothing in it was designed to survive variation.

Two things fix it. First, a cap: four metrics, one primary chart, one table. Second, states — empty, loading, error, and no permission are design work, not edge cases, and they are where a demo turns into a product.

sections.name: App shell
sections.why: Sidebar with six items maximum, current item marked by a position bar rather than colour alone. Colour-only selection disappears for anyone with a colour vision deficiency.

sections.name: Top bar
sections.why: Workspace, date range, one primary action. The date range belongs here rather than in each chart, because a dashboard whose panels disagree about the period is a dashboard nobody trusts.

sections.name: KPI row
sections.why: Exactly four. Each carries value, unit, delta with direction and comparison period, plus a sparkline. A fifth metric halves the attention available to the other four.

sections.name: Primary chart
sections.why: One question, stated in the title. Axes carry units. Three series maximum. If the title is a noun phrase like Revenue, no question has been asked.

sections.name: Secondary breakdown
sections.why: A sorted bar list of the top eight, with a link to the rest. Sorting is the analysis; presentation is not.

sections.name: Data table
sections.why: Sortable headers, sticky header row, numbers right-aligned in tabular figures. This is the section power users live in.

sections.name: Detail drawer
sections.why: Opens from a row, shows the record and its history, closes with Escape. A full page navigation loses the table position and the reader's place.

sections.name: States
sections.why: Empty with a way forward, loading as skeleton rows that match final layout, error with the failed request named, and a no-permission state. Four screens that decide whether the product feels finished.

promptLines: Build an analytics dashboard for {{DOMAIN}}.
AUDIENCE
An operator who opens this screen every morning to answer one question and then leaves. They are not exploring; they are checking. The layout must support a scan in under sixty seconds.
STRUCTURE (exactly this order)

1. App shell: fixed left sidebar, six navigation items maximum, current item marked with a 3px left bar plus weight change, not colour alone. Top bar with workspace switcher, a single global date range picker, and one primary action.
2. KPI row: exactly four metrics. Each shows the value with its unit, a delta with direction and the comparison period, and a sparkline with no axis. No fifth card.

3. Primary chart: one question, stated as the title (for example: Did activation improve after the March release?). One y-axis with a unit label, one x-axis with dates, up to three series in the legend. {{CHART}}
4. Secondary breakdown: a sorted horizontal bar list of the top eight segments with their share, and a link to the full list. Sorted descending by the metric that matters, never alphabetically.
5. Data table: {{TABLE}} Sortable headers, sticky header row, numbers right-aligned in tabular figures, 8 rows per page with a visible count.
6. Detail drawer: opens from a row click, shows the record fields and a small history list, closes with Escape and returns focus to the triggering row.
7. States: {{STATES}}
8. Settings row or panel: date range, timezone, and export. The export states its format and row limit before the click, not after.
STYLE
{{STYLE}}
DATA RULES
- Generate 40 to 60 rows of plausible data. Include one outlier, one zero, and one segment that dropped by half.
- Dates span 90 days with weekly seasonality so the chart has a shape rather than noise.
- Numbers use thousands separators; at most one decimal unless the unit requires more.
- Colour carries meaning only: one accent for the primary series, two muted tints for secondary, grey for everything else. No decorative colour.
- Every chart needs a one-sentence text summary beneath it, so the panel is readable without seeing the graphic.
CONSTRAINTS
- {{DENSITY}}
- The table must not overflow horizontally at 1280px width.
- Keyboard: every control reachable, visible focus ring, drawer closable with Escape, table rows activatable with Enter.
- Charts must remain legible at 320px wide with labels thinned rather than truncated.
- No chart without a unit. No percentage without its base.
OUTPUT
One screen, self-contained, with a mock data module at the top of the script so the numbers can be swapped in one place.

options.label: Product analytics
options.value: product analytics. The four KPIs are weekly active users, activation rate, day-30 retention and time to first value; the primary question is whether the last release changed activation.

options.label: Revenue and finance
options.value: revenue operations. The four KPIs are MRR, net revenue retention, gross margin and days sales outstanding; the primary question is which cohort is expanding and which is contracting.

options.label: Infrastructure
options.value: infrastructure monitoring. The four KPIs are error rate, p95 latency, saturation and deploy frequency; the primary question is whether the last hour is worse than the same hour yesterday.

options.label: Support operations
options.value: support operations. The four KPIs are first response time, resolution time, reopen rate and backlog age; the primary question is where the queue is accumulating this week.

options.label: Line with brush
options.value: Render the primary chart as a line chart with a range brush beneath it. Dragging the brush updates the KPI row, and the brush keeps its selection while the page is open.
options.hint: The default for time series with more than 30 points.

options.label: Stacked bars
options.value: Render the primary chart as stacked bars with at most three segments, a 2px gap between bars, and segment totals on hover only. The stack must always sum to a meaningful total.
options.hint: Use when composition matters as much as volume.

options.label: Area with comparison
options.value: Render the primary chart as an area chart of the current period with the previous period as a dashed line behind it, no fill on the comparison, and the gap described in the text summary.

options.label: Bulk actions
options.value: Include row checkboxes, a bulk action bar that appears only when rows are selected, and a count of what is selected. Destructive bulk actions require a confirmation naming the row count.
options.hint: For operational tables where the dashboard is also the tool.

options.label: Row menu
options.value: No checkboxes. A per-row overflow menu with three actions, keyboard accessible, closing on Escape or outside click.
options.hint: For read-mostly tables with occasional intervention.

options.label: Read only
options.value: No actions in the table at all. Rows open the detail drawer and nothing else. Every column is sortable and the metric column shows a delta.
options.hint: For reporting screens where editing belongs elsewhere.

options.label: All four
options.value: Implement all four states. Empty: one sentence explaining what will appear here and a link to the action that creates the first record. Loading: skeleton rows matching the final layout, no spinner. Error: the failed request named, a retry button, and the timestamp of the attempt. No permission: what the role is missing and who to ask, without a support link.

options.label: Empty and loading
options.value: Implement empty and loading states only, both matching the final layout exactly so nothing jumps when data arrives.

options.label: Comfortable
options.value: Use 44px table rows, 1rem card padding, and 16px gaps between panels. Optimised for a first-time reader rather than a daily user.

options.label: Compact
options.value: Use 32px table rows, 0.75rem card padding, 8px gaps, and 13px body text. Optimised for someone who opens this screen every morning and already knows what everything means.

options.label: Product neutral
options.value: Product neutral: white panels on a #f6f7f9 canvas, 1px borders in #e3e7ec, 8px radii, one blue accent for the primary series and interactive elements, no shadows except on the drawer.

options.label: Dark console
options.value: Dark console: #0e1116 canvas, #151a21 panels, 1px borders at 9 percent white, one cyan accent, monospace for all numbers, no rounded corners above 4px.

options.label: Swiss reporting
options.value: Swiss reporting: white canvas, black rules at 1px, no panels at all — sections separated by rules only, one red accent for the primary series, all labels uppercase at 0.7rem with 0.08em tracking.

change.note: Change this first and change the metric names with it. A dashboard called Revenue but populated with session counts is the most obvious tell that a template was reused.
Line with brush suits long time series; stacked bars suit composition; area with comparison suits period-over-period. Picking the wrong one is why a correct chart still answers nothing.
Bulk actions require a real selection model, so only choose them if the screen is genuinely operational. A read-only table with excellent sorting beats a half-wired bulk bar.
The four-state version is what makes the screen look built rather than generated. If you only have time for two, do empty and loading — they are the ones users hit first.
Comfortable for onboarding and marketing screenshots, compact for daily use. Do not mix: compact rows inside comfortable panels reads as an accident.

builders.name: v0
builders.note: Generate the shell and KPI row first, then ask for the chart, then the table. Whole-screen generations produce inconsistent panel heights that are tedious to fix afterwards.

builders.name: Lovable
builders.note: It will add a seventh KPI unless the cap is explicit. Also check the chart axes — it tends to omit units, which is the defect that makes a dashboard unusable rather than unattractive.

builders.name: Bolt
builders.note: State the charting approach (hand-rolled SVG, or a named library) or you will get an inline dependency you cannot audit. For a demo, hand-rolled SVG is smaller and more controllable.

builders.name: Cursor / Claude Code
builders.note: Ask for a mock data module first, then the components. Iterating on layout against fixed data is far faster than regenerating data with every change.

failures.title: Seven KPI cards of equal weight
failures.body: Equal size communicates equal importance, which is almost never true. Four metrics with one clearly dominant beats seven with none. The cap is the design decision.

failures.title: Charts without units
failures.body: An unlabelled y-axis turns a chart into decoration. Revenue in what currency, latency in milliseconds or seconds, rate as a percentage of what base. Without units the panel cannot be read, only admired.

failures.title: Fake data that hides layout bugs
failures.body: Three rows of nearly identical numbers never reveals overflow, truncation or a delta label colliding with a value. Include an outlier, a zero and a very long segment name — those are what break the layout in production.

failures.title: No empty state
failures.body: A new account opens the dashboard and sees blank panels, which reads as broken rather than new. The empty state is the first screen most users ever see.
